problem: Prior human-in-the-loop and language-guided navigation methods mostly rely on RL policies needing rich human-in-the-loop datasets, and do not decide when to ask for help or convert language feedback into waypoints in a known map that changes at runtime (e.g., closed doors).
motivation: In real deployments (precision agriculture, construction, persistent monitoring) a map is known a priori but the environment changes, which can trap autonomous planners in local minima. A human can easily resolve such situations if the robot asks at the right time and can understand natural-language guidance.
key_idea: Trigger a human query when the re-planned global path length deviates by more than 25% from the previous plan, then parse the natural-language feedback via a VLMap (CLIP features, GMM-based match thresholding) into candidate waypoints and pick the shortest path through a graph of them.
insight: A simple, training-free path-length deviation monitor is enough to detect significant blockages without a learned policy, but it misses gradual changes (factory Route 3 SR drops to 0.80 because the plan changed too gradually to trigger a query). Fitting a GMM to VLMap scores and taking the highest-mean component avoids needing background-class queries. Failures arise when multiple similar features compete (factory Route 2 RMSE 3.056), suggesting follow-up clarification queries.
method: Query Decision Module: re-computes global plan at 5 Hz and compares its length with the previous plan; if the deviation exceeds threshold tau=25%, asks the human for feedback.
Map Query Module: scores each VLMap cell's CLIP feature against the CLIP text embedding of each feedback phrase (inner product).
GMM matching: fits a k-component Gaussian mixture to scores across the map; cells belonging to the highest-mean component are matches; morphological filtering yields contiguous regions.
Waypoint sampling: for each region, takes free-space points within a fixed radius, computes clearance to obstacles, samples a waypoint from max-clearance points; gives candidate sets per phrase.

Waypoint Selection Module: builds a directed graph (robot pose + candidates, edges only between sequential phrases, weights = map travel distance, close pairs pruned) and runs Floyd-Warshall to select the shortest path ending at any last-phrase candidate.
Map construction: GMapping (sim) or Cartographer (real) for occupancy grid and poses, aligned with the RGB-D-built VLMap; conventional navigation stack handles planning/control.

numbers_note: Custom small-scale evaluations only; no standard benchmarks or baseline comparisons. Tables were duplicated in source.
results: On Gazebo the method reaches SR 1.00 in Small House (RMSE 0.470) and 0.93 in Factory (RMSE 1.456); on a real RosBot it gets SR 0.79 and RMSE 0.964. Language-only waypoint generation yields higher RMSE (1.215 / 2.247). No baseline comparison is reported.
limitations: Path-length deviation trigger misses gradual changes, causing failures (factory SR 0.80 on one route)
Ambiguity when multiple similar features match a phrase leads to wrong waypoints; no clarification queries yet
Sensitive to pose noise/VLMap alignment; small-scale tests with no baselines, and onboard compute caused out-of-order messages in real world
